taken before. What foul old age has so suddenly
seized you and broken your spirits and taken away your wraths?
Either with me, young men, come, go through the midst of the city
and the Argolic band, or fall before your dear sons.'
He rushes in and fiercely summons his fathers' shades to his enterprise:
'Holy Voraptus, my father, supply now to your son
your courage and an equal spirit, if to you, hating
the fates, the slow and shameful delays no less did I myself
obey, and the small grandsons have learned the same.'
This he says, and is heard in Erebus. Then he seizes his sword,
turbid, and burning with his fathers' furies shakes his arms.
Aquites, consecrated to the native waters and priest of great
Phasis, wandered in northern arms
(the honour of his brow is of poplar, and his temples are seen
bound with the gray-green bough), longing to lead you, Cyrnus,
forgetful of your father, from the harsh fight;
and now ranging unhurt through all the throngs and the scattered
lines, he sees his son nowhere, and as he enters again
crying out, again ranges the different parts of the war,
and his driven lance rings about his sea-blue fillets.
Fierce Gesander overwhelms him with reins let loose.
He, trembling, stretched out his hand and his vain sacred emblems
and said: 'You, by this, I beg, if a father awaits you,
by your gray hairs, check your threats, and if you have a son,
spare mine.' He spoke. Against this the victor with sword driven in
replies thus: 'The father whom you think still survives for me
in shameful old age, himself chose to fall by this right hand
and of his own accord to break off the sluggish bounds.
And if you had a son's piety, if a right hand,
you would not now wear away the hours in the midst of war with prayers,
about to be the prey of dogs. For a youth every lot is fairer:
it is fitting both to have striven by hand and to have lacked a tomb.'
He had spoken; the other, dying, prays to the gods and heaven
that no such right hand should meet his wretched son.
You too, Canthus, Argo, not unaware of your death,
wept for as you snatched your weapons from the unwilling ship.
Now, pitiable one, you had reached the Scythian gulfs, now the river
of Phasis, and the day was not far when you would see the captured
fleece and the Euboean fires from your native mountains.
Him, when in the clash Gesander overwhelms with unequal
strife, he terrifies with these words: 'You who thought these homes
of men easy, Argive, here, wretched one, you behold another year
and the nursing snow and the swift weariness of life.
We have not learned either to fit our arms to the light oars
or to wait, a task, for favouring winds;
we go on horses, where the sea stiffens even in mid-flood
or the Hister roars with its swollen water; nor do your walls
please us: I am borne now free over the northern fields,
holding all, all my love with me, and the loss of a wagon alone,
nor will you long, as victor, possess this plunder.
But for feasts, whatever beast, whatever of the wild creatures.
Send to Asia, send charges to the Argolic colonists,
that they tremble not; never will I leave these winters, these rocks,
the fields of Mars, where by so savage a river we have hardened
our offspring and our rude sons, where so great a store of death
is for the men. Thus it is sweet to make war in our native frosts
and to plunder, and take this such a right hand.'
He spoke, and the missile, nourished by the Edonian winds,
he hurls; it goes through the middle of the breast, and the deadly
steel and the bristling bronze in their knot. Trembling, Idas flies up above
and at once the son of Oeneus and likewise Menoetius and he
who returned victor nearer from the Bebrycian host.
But Telamon far off raised his huge round shield,
covering you, Canthus, lifeless; as a lion, hedged in a strait,
sets his cubs behind his back, so close at hand stands
the Aeacid and holds his step, and against the rushing foe
wheels round the mass strong with sevenfold hide.
Nor less from here presses the Scythian band, and the arms of Canthus
each demands for himself and a penalty from the Greek body.
Hence a steep labour, and over the body in the middle the fight
is joined. As when, with a great whirlwind, the winds
break themselves on the threshold of Aeolia herself,
which the rage of the sea, which the clouds, and which that day
should follow: so the men's fight clings close at hand, straining,
nor can they be driven from the body they have seized.
As one who breaks a bull's hide with much oil
gives it to his servants, they stretch it, and in turn by their pulling
tame the bull's back, the ground flows with the rich grease:
such is the labour on both sides, and snatched along the narrow line
the man's pitiable limbs go: these strain against,
those against, and the alternate right hands of the men do not yield.
Hence Telamon snatches Canthus by the middle, hence burning Gesander
holds the man's neck and the soft reins of the helmet,
which, slipping to the ground, rang and cheated his right hand.
He, wicked, again rams against the orb of the sevenfold
shield and follows Canthus and demands Canthus back,
whom a hand snatches from behind, his comrade, and, received,
sets in the chariot of the maiden Euryale. She herself flies up
and at once the Haemonidae, and all the band against Gesander
alone goes. He, when he sees the new lines and the maiden's
arms, 'Shall we war even against these?' he says;
'Alas, the shame.' Then he strikes Lyce at the edge of the breast,
then Thoe, where the shield is bare; and now he was going for Harpe,
scarcely drawing her first horns with the light string,
and for Menippe, stretching the reins of her falling horse:
when the queen, doubling the axe heavy with knots and gold,
shatters part of her head and her wild-beast helmet.
Here alike a vast mass of weapons goes against one;
he for long suffices against the hurled spears,
nay, even heavier and with a nod . . .
lacking it terrified Idas;
then he falls as the side of a mountain or as the engine of a wall,
which long worn down by rocks and beams and by flames
at last sank and brought down a huge city.

title: Argonautica
text:
Behold, thinking the place and time had come and that now his own
battles were demanded, Ariasmenes brings in his scythed axles
and at once spreads the savage yokes of his comrades, about
to snatch all the Greek-born from the line, all the Colchians.
As if Jupiter, hating the race of Pyrrha, should again pour
the seas and all his reins of the flood,
that the steep ridges of Parnassus should lie hidden, pine-bearing
Othrys should yield, and the Alps shrink with their crags sunk:
with such a flood and equal destructions Ariasmenes presses,
snatching his chariots with no distinction.
Then for the first time the maiden raised the aegis and the breath
of Medusa, squalid with thrice a hundred savage snakes,
which the horses alone saw. Huge dread seizes them,
the men shaken off onto their backs, and they turn back the dire
plague upon their comrades, not willingly. Then with hooked swords
discord entangles and tears the panicked chariots.
As when most savage Tisiphone stirs the Roman
legions and the kings, whose lines flash with javelins
on either side, whose eagles, and whose parents till the same
fields, the same fields which unhappy Tiber had sent
chosen from all, not to these battles:
so but now concordant and seeking foreign fates,
the Palladian terrors snatched them away, so, turned to their own
deaths, the axles clash though their masters call them back.
Not such foul bands of men did the south winds cast up
on the Laurentine lands, nor such the image on the Libyan
shore, when the seas roll over the broken ships.
Here the yoked horses, there the masters' limbs are stretched,
which the spokes, which the reins cut, and the chariot drags
and is dragged, dripping with slaughter, and in the black dust the kings'
entrails cling now to some, now to other chariots.
Nowhere is there spirit in the Colchians, nor . . .
weapons, but the entangled and bound in the wretched bane
they stab through, and no other form of death arises
than when a hunter seeks stags not with the devouring Umbrian hound,
nor with the feathered shaft, but finds them clinging by their lofty
horns and takes them, bound fast, with blind wrath.
Bold Ariasmenes himself, his arms gathered up,
leaps down; the line of the curved scythe cuts him on every side
and parts him with the wheels, and snatched thence onto the raging
yokes, he touched the Circaean fields no more.
Such deaths the Minyae and the scattered Cytaeans
were mingling in rivalry on the fields, and pressing Scythia,
when Juno, seeing that this was not the way to the fleece
for the son of Aeson, nor were returns to be thus prepared,
the queen sets in motion the last resource, before the treacherous
king lays open his deadly counsels and savage wraths.
She upbraids Vulcan, sorrowful, with late complaints,
whose flame-breathing bulls she sees among the royal
pastures, breathing Tartarean night from their breast.
For lest, the war finished, he bid the Minyae yoke
these monsters and sow with the teeth of the Cadmean serpent,
she fears for the day and looks about for various arts.
Medea alone comes to her mind, all her thought on one
maiden, than whom none is more powerful at the nocturnal altars.
At her addresses and the juices scattered through the pathless places
the fixed stars are afraid, and the orbit of her grandsire the Sun is amazed.
She changes the fields and the river's ways, her own fire binds
all things, sleep revives parents wearied with age
and gives the distaffs other lengths without law. Her even mighty Circe
marvelled at, with her terrifying measures, her the stranger Phrixus,
although he knew the moon to foam with Atracian poison
and shades to be stirred by Haemonian songs.
Therefore Juno seeks to join, dread with magic powers
and virginity, the Colchian as ally to the Greek leader.
For she sees none other equal against the bulls and the springing
arms, nor one who would stand in the midst of the line of flame:
to dread no crime in her mind, no sights.
What if blind love and savage fire be added?
Hence she seeks the bridal halls of Venus and the roofs ever fresh
with garlands. At her sight the goddess long since leaps up
from the high couches, and all the host of the winged Loves.
And first Saturnia, as suppliant, approaches her with calm
words, fearing to lay open her true fears.
'Now in your hands is our hope and all power,'
she says; 'consent to this the more to one telling the truth.
As the harsh Tirynthian is exiled from the Argolic shores,
my mind is not the same as Jove's, and his will opposed,
no honour to my bridal chamber or its fires of old in the night.
Grant, I pray, the alluring breathings of cunning beauty
and your adornments powerful on earth and in heaven.'
The goddess felt the guile, long since of her own accord seeking
the Colchian and to cut off all the race of hated Phoebus.
Then indeed she gains her wishes, nor, suffering her to pray
further, she gave the keen grace and the girdle fertile
in monsters, in which is no piety nor care for fame,
no modesty, but on the contrary light and hasty desire
and the address of evil and sweet error for the wavering
and fear and the mad care of another's peril.
'All my empire and all the arms of my sons,'
she says, 'I have given; now shake what minds you please.'

title: Argonautica
text:
Saturnia is girded, glad, with the secret poisons,
and hence comes to the inmost chamber of the maiden's seat,
imitating her sister Chalciope in sound and form.
The divinity shone from afar against her will, and dread at once
struck her limbs and a huge horror smote the daughter of Aeetes.
'So do you not know, sister,' she says, 'that the Minyae have come
hither over unknown waves, and that not only to our father
have they joined allied hands? But the rest of the throng
holds the walls and enjoys the men's heavenly arms,
while you sit idle in your chamber, you alone fixed
in your father's house? When will it be yours to see such kings?'
She nothing in reply; for the goddess did not suffer it, but clasps
her hand and bears the marvelling one off with rapid steps.
The unhappy maiden is led to the topmost walls, ignorant
of the evil to come, and entrusted to a false sister:
as white lilies shine especially through the vernal
colours, whose life is short and all their honour
blooms but a little while, and now the South wind with dusky wings threatens.
Her, sitting in the high groves, Hecate, child of Perses,
wept for, and gave forth these voices from the depth of her breast:
'You leave, alas, our grove and the bands of your peers,
ah wretched one, that you may wander, not of your will, to the Greek cities,
yet not unbidden; nor will I leave you, my care.
You shall give great memorials of your flight, nor anywhere
shall you be despised, a captive to a lying man, and he shall feel
me your mistress and shall grieve at the shameful theft of a handmaid.'
She had spoken. But they make for the edges of the walls
and, fixed, shudder at the crashes of men and trumpets,
as, sad at the threatening cold of the storm-clouds,
birds come up to the branches and cling in fear.
Now the Getae, now all Iberia and the Drangaean legion
fall in a dense slaughter and are strewn over the wide fields.
Half-dead and doubled among their own weapons and their own
horses, they roll over in wretched struggle a savage
heap and fill the fields with long sobbings.
Against them the victorious Geloni redouble their fathers'
paean; soon the same joys return to the vanquished,
where the god and the better image of war looks back.
Who would have given such deaths, who such deeds,
say now, and you, Muse, recall the fierce frenzy.
Absyrtus, flashing with the rays of his shield and the chariot
of his grandsire the Sun, whose quivering spear close at hand
the races could not behold, nor his menacing helmet,
but they return trembling and take wounds in the turned
back and increase their flight with great cries,
tramples the heavy lines with his charge and strews the bodies
with his high horses and stifles the groans of the breathing heap.
Nor does Aron accompany him lighter, over whose bristling
parti-coloured arms and limbs squalid with bronze
a barbaric cloak blazes with embroidery, and, shaken by the wind,
fills out the horse, as Lucifer goes on rosy wings,
whom Venus rejoices to lead forth in the bright heaven.
But not far from there Rambelus and keen Otaxes
had scattered the Colchians, and likewise inglorious Armes,
accustomed with a new trick to ravage the stalls and the herds
with unpunished thefts, had increased his brow with horns,
shaggy, and had hidden in the terror of the Lycaean god:
with this guise then he had fixed the astonished foes.
Whom, as soon as Aron saw moving the wars with their known
fright, 'Do you now think,' he says, 'that you have sought
frightened herdsmen and a stupid flock? Neither pastures nor an ox
are here for you; send these illusions to your nocturnal robberies
and feign no god to me; a god too, join your right hand.'
So he speaks, and aiming the missile with foot set forward,
directs it, and as the hairs slipped the wounds lay open.
Nor less the Aeetian offspring of Aeolian Phrixus
is borne raging himself too, and now glad shows himself
to the Cytaean lines, now to his kindred Achaeans.
And when in the midst of the trial of the hard war Jason
saw these rejoicing in their very praises,
'Blessed,' he says, 'O our race and now sure offspring
of the house of Aeolus, unlooked-for; great enough are the gifts
of toil I bring, enough do I repay all things by this sight.'
He spoke, and against Suetes and the fate of great Ceramnus
he flashed out, and whirling his shield throws down this one
with his knee cut, opens that one with a wide gash through the breast.
Argus stretches both from their horses with a huge daring,
Zacorus and Phalces, and on foot, a footman, drains Amastris.
That barbarian bears clots of blood and his spilled entrails
and, hissing with empty wrath, sinks down.
Calais gives Barisas to death and Rhipeus, ever attending
the near battles with venal blood, a warrior who bargained
a hundred chosen oxen, a hundred horses; with these
the cruel one repays his soul and the light; at last, now bereft,
he looks back into the sweet air, and no treasure can buy back heaven.
He sinks, through his temples the sea-blue twisted locks,
even then veiled with his mother's reed, Peucon.
But his mother Maeotis alike from the deepest caverns
filled the lakes with wailing and called her son,
now no longer flying along the banks, now not over the curving
pools, nor cutting off the stags in the midst of the marble.
Eurytus drives the Exomatae over the plain. On Nestor's spear
youthful Helix dies, nor was the nourishment given back
to his dear father, and he is snatched away in his short years.
But Latagus and Zetes, Daraps; that one he dispatches with the spear,
this one he flees, when he saw the huge wave of sudden blood
and the breast gleaming with the point at its end.

title: Argonautica
text:
But behold, Medea, seated on her father's walls,
while she surveys the single contests of the great war
and herself recognizes these kings afar in the dense gloom
and seeks others with Juno as her teacher,
catches sight of the Aesonian head far off, and at once
brings her keen eyes and senses and favouring mind hither,
now seeing beforehand whither he might snatch himself, now
whither, turning, he might go off, and how many horses, how many arms
he, one man, might scatter, and how with how dense spears
he might halt the wandering men.
And wherever she scatters again her wandering eyes with silent face,
seeking either her brother's or her betrothed husband's arms,
there fierce and alone Jason meets the wretched one.
Then she addresses her sister with these words, as if ignorant:
'Who, I pray, is this, who long since I behold burning over all
the field, whom you yourself too see? For you also at such
valour I think astonished.' Against this harsh Juno
replies, driving with goads and pressing with dire deceits:
'The very son of Aeson you behold, sister, who over so great
a sea seeks again the owed fleece of his kinsman Phrixus,
nor now is any first in the glory of race or in blood.
You see how among the Minyae and the Cytaean nobles
he flashes shining, and over what great heaps he leaps;
and now he will set sail, now he will leave our shores,
seeking the riches of happy Thessaly and the fields
beloved by Phrixus. Let him go, and would that he overcame his labours.'
Having said only this, she urges her to gaze more on the fields,
while it is given, and to run over the man's ardent fights;
but at once the goddess with her words drove this one, that one with favouring
Mars, and drove new strength beneath his breast.
His face beneath the lofty peak of his cone has long
flashed savage, and he kindles in his course, nor to you, Perses,
nor to you, maiden, is the crest a glad star of the Achaean,
keen as the autumn dog, and the comets summoned by angry
Jove to the unjust realm, fatal.
Nor did his own goddess escape the son of Cretheus, and he feels
a fresh force driven through his limbs and lifts himself above the lines,
as great as when Caucasus himself grows white with frost
and a great rain and goes off, wintry, into the highest north.
Then indeed, as a lion rages in the rich folds,
luxuriating, and scatters his hunger and changes his slaughters,
so neither fierce in one part nor lingering in one death
is he, turbulent, and rages alike on all, and now with savage
sword, now with hostile spear the fights grow thin.
Then both Hebrus, surging with terrifying locks,
and Getic Prion he strikes; he snatches the head of Auchus
and the arms and sends them to roll on the vast sands.
But the son of Jove, Colaxes, had filled out his fates;
and now the father saddens the stars with mournful face,
moving in vain his sick breast with such cares:
'Ah me, if I should strive to withdraw my son from the harsh
lot and dare to trust in my realms,
the brother of Amycus still mourning his death, and all the throng
of the gods would roar, whose sons have fallen and shall fall.
Nay, let each have his own day, and I will deny to all
what I deny to myself.' Thus speaking, he heaps the last honours
on the wretched one and fills him with great spirit, about to die.
He flies over the fields and mingles measureless deaths
through the wedges, as the rain, burst from the wintry bow,
driving rocks and the ruins of woods and of works,
until, having raged from the huge peak of the mountain,
it is broken and little by little fails into a new river.
Such is the offspring of Jove, flashing in his last hour,
and now he marks the great-hearted Hypetaon and Gessithous,
now Arines and Olbus; now, wounded Apres
and, deserted by his horse, Thydrus on foot he dispatches with the spear,
Phasiades, whom Caucasus, guardian of his father's flock by custom,
begot at the first waves of Phasis;
hence the boy had his surname, and his parents called him the servant
of Phasis with his uncut hair, in vain.
And now he pressed fiercely on others, when the unjust goddess
breaks his last distaff, and victorious Jason comes.
He receives him, speaking thus with savage voice, Colaxes:
'You, wretches, have you come hither to glut the Scythian dogs
and the Scythian birds?' he says, and a rock he seized,
the burden of his right hand and of that age,
he heaves up from the shaken earth, which royal Juno
turned aside to the unknown head and the unwept fate of Moneses.
Headlong he falls; Jupiter did not turn the blow from his son,
but the fatal wound of the Aesonian spear
goes through the shield, through the breast, and to him fallen the bloody
son of Aeson flies and embitters the dying man's death.
He is scattered hence, and now known comes to the wretched Alani.

title: Argonautica
text:
But the queen pursues the man (for the god does not remove the fire),
gazing, and clings with burning eyes;
and now less glad at the image of the present fight,
she chides her fears and the cares she fosters unknowing,
looking back, whether her sister be true; nor does she dare,
fierce, to believe the false face, and again into the same joys
she slides and is drawn by the sweetness of the savage flame.
And as the light south wind plays before the leaves and the topmost
tops of the wood with gentle breaths, but the wretched
keels straightway felt it monstrous,
so is Medea driven to the utmost furies.
Sometimes she handles the necklaces torn from the alluring
goddess and fits them, blazing, to her wretched neck,
and wherever the maddening gold gave through her tender limbs,
she faints; and the maiden returns the goddess's adornments,
troubled not by the gems, not by the light metal,
but by the torches, by the mass of the god, whom now with all
her breast she holds; the last modesty wanders on her rosy face.
And first to her: 'Do you believe, O sister, that the father will give
the promises, to whom the Argolic guest came with the gods
more kindly? Or how much of the bitter war now remains?
Alas, to what perils for an unknown race he flings
himself.' To her speaking thus in the midst of her words Juno
left, now powerful in her enterprise and secure of her guile.
The shameless maiden leans more boldly from the high walls
and does not follow the sister borne off, nor seek her.
But as often as the hard force of the leaders and the men, dense,
suddenly pressed the son of Aeson, and when all the shower
went against one, so often is he beaten with rocks and spears:
and first at hostile Lexanor's bow she shuddered,
but the arrow goes high over the Aesonian head
and seeks you, Caicus; the pitiable wife is left to Caicus
and the home unfinished at its first bridal.
Royal Myraces, an interpreter, had come from the eastern shores,
to join the Colchians, far off, and the Aeetian covenants
with the Parthians, not in vain, with gold given.
Then the Fates held the youth in the Cytaean lands
and the love of sudden Mars. With him went his armour-bearer,
a half-man, bearing an unripe and barren youth.
He himself, sitting on Euphratean carpets at the reins,
now light runs forward into the lines in his hostile car,
now in flight scatters his feigned, turned arrows.
But green with gems and the thread of the eastern wood
he binds his father's tiara at the very edge of his neck,
notable for his sleeves, notable for the scimitar on his right;
the wanton coverings of the barbarian foot run forward.
Nor long did those spoils escape savage Syene,
and through the smooth tiger, stained with much purple,
the driven point goes; sudden blood from her mouth
the wounded tiger drives and pours out her master's life;
the boy himself, his bow broken, twines his head bowed down.
Then with black blood the fiery cloak, with blood the face
and the heavy locks grew wet, which with Sabaean flower
his parent had nourished and marked with liquid gold.
As one whom by waters and the richness of fertile earth
rears, and fills with favouring winds, an olive,
and neither his constant labour nor his hope fails the nourisher,
and now he sees the first leaf from the tender crown,
when suddenly headlong, with storm-clouds let loose, the northern
winter comes and stretches it, torn up, on the black sand:
not otherwise before the city Myraces and before the very
face of the maiden falls; but she is moved no more,
sick with fear for the one, than she sees you, Meleager, raging,
than Talaus, or marvels at the fights of Acastus;
but enough did the very races and the fields see these
in like storm press upon the routed squadrons:
before her eyes is the late flight of the leaders and the abundant
blood of the falling, and the chariots emptied of their huge masters.

title: Argonautica
text:
Perses did not bear these groans and the slaughter of his own
and the turned backs, and fills heaven with these complaints:
'Why now, cast out from my native seats, that I might raise
these fights and move Scythia to war,
you gods, you have mocked me with an empty augury?
What did your omens, Jupiter, promise me of my brother's
deserved end? For me you were preparing, forsooth, the Argive
help and to join such great strength.
Cruel indeed is the delay of light to the wretched; yet let the fates,
I pray, give me that one day, on which I may see the Achaeans
who deserved the fleece so, and this man too, proud in valour,
the son of Aeson, weeping his so great labours without honour.'
He had spoken, and beats his breast with his own arms
and fills his helmet with weeping, his helmet with sobs;
and he was going headlong into the fires of the mid-battle,
had not Pallas first seen him from the opposing arms
and to herself: 'Lo, fierce Perses rushes into death,
whom his father has now resolved to set over the Colchians and the throne
of his brother. I fear lest, slain by our guile,
he upbraid us and repay this fault with great terror.'
Saying this, she spreads a mist with her black mantle
and removes the hissing spears from about the man's head.
He, over his allied races, is lifted in a gentle whirlwind
and, snatched a little into the light air,
now at last is borne down to the farthest edges of the fight,
where by chance the late Iberian and the Issedonian phalanxes
lack Mars and aid the line with shouts alone.
Night at the same time, longed for, brings forth her star-bearing shades;
and at once the crash of war falls, and sick from the walls
the maiden departs, having long endured a lengthy fear.
As the wild Thyiads pause a little amid the rites of Nyctelius,
then snatched the god, now now ready for whatever,
with no other tumult does Medea return,
and amid the Greek lines and the native phalanxes
ever with unsatisfied cares she recognizes Jason
and his arms and whatever face is left from the hollow helmet.
7. The Argonautica of Gaius Valerius Flaccus, Book Seven.
You too the late evening now parts from your Thessalian guest,
and now your joys, O maiden, are leaving you,
and night comes rushing down, no friend to one who loves alone.
So when, with feet that lingered on the threshold's edge,
she reached her sick bed and her mind took fire in the dark,
then through long sleeplessness she turned her shifting laments,
trying to learn from what sickness she suffered, and at last she dared
to confess a little to herself, and spoke thus in her grief:
'Now by what chance, or thus forever wakeful,
am I, willing, dragged into my own wandering? Surely this night
was not mine before I saw your face, O bravest of young men.
Why do I, mad, recall it again and again,
parted by so wide a sea? What is this stranger alone
to my mind? Let him rather take now the fleece of my kinsman Phrixus,
which alone he seeks and which is the single cause
of his toil. For when will he look again upon these halls?
And when will my father journey to the cities of Aeson's land?
Happy are they who dared to give themselves to the open waves
and did not fear such roads, nor, having followed such a man,
this man and then a husband—yet even so, let such a one depart.'
Then, tossed upon her couch, having tried the whole bed over,
behold, she sees the threshold whiten with the faint dawn;
and the risen light refreshed the sleepless lover no less
than when a gentle shower lifts the drooping ears of grain
and welcome breezes now come down to oars grown weary.
But now their care for the long voyages reminds the Minyae,
and in that very hour, in vain, they seek the king
to claim their joy and their reward. Jason, allowing them
first to make their vows and kindle their captured spoils to the gods,
leans forward and holds his eyes afar, to see whether already
the golden fleece and the hall grow bright with the offered wool.
But the king, just as Jason is making ready his look and his words,
forestalls him, breaks off delay, and into the very face
of the man who lingers leaps, and pours himself out in such wrath:
'You, sown in another world, having your own shores and realms,
what madness drove you across so many waves to these coasts?
What so great a love of me? You are the first cause of my ills,
you, Phrixus, my son-in-law. Would that the sea had drowned you
as it did your sister, that I, happy, might know no Greeks
by name. What king is Pelias, what Thessalian, or what
is Greece, what race of men do I behold, or where are the rocks
of the Cyaneae? See, a guest has come into Scythian coasts.
That fifty exiles—shame, alas—should Jason have pierced through to Asia,
and that he alone should so scorn me above all others,
one ship alone, to carry off plunder from a living king?
Let him bid me offer my own groves, bid me throw them open,
and think it worth no war at all to win his victory!
Why not, come, snatch the consecrated gifts from all the temples,
and lead away the very daughters from their parents' arms,
O robber, if you please? Should I believe you have homes,
have parents—you whom one ship alone feeds on unspeakable
plunder, you whom cruel storm sustains, and whom—if we trust them—
their own king dashed against the sea and forbade to return?
No doubt that he might gain the gold of the Aeolian ram!
Sooner shall my Caucasus sink down with its shade cut away,
and sooner shall it seek again the Haemonian spoils beyond the sea,
or sooner shall I set up Helle with funeral fillets
. . . Yet if you persist otherwise, refusing to yield this land,
and shame at a fruitless return stirs you, and there lies hidden
in one ship I know not what greater purpose than its men, I myself
will not hold back what you seek; only fulfil my command first.
Before the city lies a field of Mars, rough with long years,
and bulls that breathe fire and that once knew me too as I pressed
the plough, bulls that even now are slow at times to know me.
To these our old age has now given more and more its fury
and rankness, and their fire, prouder than its wont,
roars from the mouth. Succeed, O bravest, to my glory,
and cultivate my fields, my guest. Nor will the seed be wanting
that I once sowed myself, nor the harvests I alone reaped.
One night is enough for counsel; turn over with yourself,
and with your own gods, these my commands; and if there is in that
strength of yours aught, you will come to the fields of the foretold toil.
I myself, still uncertain, could wish you straightway wrapped
in those shadows and those flames, or rather to hold out a while,
until you cast the seed upon the ploughed field,
and until the Cadmean serpent's soldiery springs from your teeth
and the new-broken furrows flower with an armed crop.'
His daughter, first to wonder at the savage tyrant's voice,
stopped, and turned her pale face toward the young man,
and trembled with fear, lest in ignorance the stranger dare,
and lest, poor wretch, he think himself able. Horror had gripped
even him, and he stood fixed in sullen anger.
Not so does the Tyrrhenian and Ionian helmsman stand dazed,
who, even as he watches you, Tiber, and the bright lighthouse
on its serene height, suddenly sees the harbor nowhere, nowhere
Ausonia, and the cruel Syrtes drawing near.
Yet then he gathers what answers to give the monstrous tyrant,
and at last rises from his deep brooding gaze.
'You did not,' he says, 'O Aeetes, give this homecoming, not this
hope, to the Minyae, when first before your walls we took up
arms for you. Where is your faith now turned? What guiles do your
commands roll over? I see another Pelias here, other seas.
Come then, all of you, press upon this head with a tyrant's
hatreds and commands; never will my right hand fail me, nor my hope;
my way is to endure commands and not to yield to hardship.
One thing I ask: whether that crop overwhelm me with its spears,
or tomorrow's fire devour me with its opposing jaws,
let a messenger be sent from here to the cruel ears of Pelias,
that here the heroes perished, and that I, had there been any faith
in you, might have been brought back home to my fatherland.'
At such words he leaves both daughter and father stunned,
and headlong rushes out from the faithless hall.
But trembling, and forsaken amid her parents,
the maiden is silent, and could not keep her eyes fixed
a moment on the ground, nor keep from turning her sorrowing face;
she looked back at the doors and still found him departing,
and the stranger, alas, then seemed more beautiful to the wretched lover
as he left: such shoulders, such a back he leaves behind.
She longs that he, and the very doorposts, would come on a little,
and she holds her burning steps within the threshold.
As when wandering Io feels the last sands of the shore
and bears her foot back and forth, whom the Fury drives
to cross the swelling seas, and the matrons of Pharos call across the deep:
not otherwise she circles and hangs about the open doors,
in case a kinder father should call the Minyae back; and seeking
the face of the stranger, she grieves, faint upon his lonely bed,
or comes into the lap of her dear sister and shrinks away again,
and tries to speak, then falls silent, and again withdrawing
asks how the stranger Phrixus came to settle on Aeaean shores,
how the winged dragons carried off Circe.
Then in pity she takes joy in the sight of her companions
and cannot have her fill, and suddenly clings to her parents
more fondly, and presses kisses upon her father's hand.
So a dog, used to the couch and to her master's sweet table,
sick now with a new plague and the madness to come,
before her flight roams, whimpering, through all the house.
At last she chides herself thus in tender anger:
'You go on, madwoman,' she says, 'and his image torments you,
and your care for him, who perhaps in flight holds the high keel,
and who will carry off my name, not his, to his native cities.
Yet why does he so move me—whether he overcomes the labors
or falls, and Greece is troubled with so great a grief?
At least, if the last fates were already bearing off the hero,
would he had been bidden rather to go to tyrants unknown,
O would he were, and were not dying at last in this city.
For he is said to be of the blood of our starry Phrixus,
and I saw my dear sister grieve for him,
and she says that he, poor man, was driven by commands to cross these waves.
But let him return by whatever means, and let him not know
that I prayed thus, and let him not hate my father.'
She had said this, and had flung her heavy limbs upon the bed,
if pitying rest would come, when sleep, more savage still,
troubles and drives her: here the suppliant guest is stretched out,
here her father. She breaks her slumbers with fresh dread
and rises from the couch; she knows her handmaids and dear home,
but a moment ago swept through Thessalian cities:
as Orestes, distraught with the avenging Furies and blind terrors,
snatches his sword and strikes the ranks of his cruel mother;
the serpents shake him, the wrath of the dread-sounding scourge shakes him,
and again he believes he rages, driving on to the slaughter
of the hostile Spartan woman, and returns wearied from the false carnage
of the goddesses, and collapses into his wretched sister's face.
When Juno sees the Colchian wavering with these cares
in vain, and not yet yielding to the final frenzy,
she no longer keeps the borrowed face and voice
of Chalciope. Since her ardor grows dull and shame the lighter
. . . and her mind set firm against the evil, she is borne aloft
into the thin air and seeks out Venus on golden Olympus.
'I remember how you shared the labor with me;
but she remains too hard, and turned to wrath
and frenzy she grieves, and now, deceived, has left me.
Go, I pray, and conquer that love by which she mocks me,
conquer it, I pray, that she may dare at last to escape
her father's house, and by some chance defend my Aeson's son
from every peril: that power lies in the sacred poison she trusts.
And the serpent, too, that stands guard the whole night through,
who fills all his grove and the golden fleece (look further on)
with so many coils, so many windings—
let her beguile him, and loose him into sleep from the great ash tree.
This is yours; the rest I entrust to the Furies and to her.'
Then Venus, mother of the winged Loves, speaks thus:
'Nor when you first set out to bend the maiden's senses
and to touch her soul with an unknown care
were we wanting to you, since at once my girdle was given to her,
the soil shaken, so that she gave way, dislodged from her place.
That is not enough; my own self is needed, and her hesitating
heart demands me, and her wavering shame: I will soon make her
herself seek the bond of Aeson's son and fear delay.
You—let her come quickly to the shrine of light-bearing Diana,
where the Colchian woman is wont to pour out the sacred torches
and circle her mistress with an even troop of companions.
And let no fear of Hecate come upon you now, nor fear
that by chance I hinder your enterprise; rather I desire that she dare:
love will pass at once, and with triple-tongued chant
I will force her to subdue the very fire-breathing bulls.'
. . . and with an embrace she seeks; then she sees winged Iris,
and bids her hasten to obey the bidding of Dione
and set the son of Aeson in the appointed grove.
Straightway from here Iris sought the Minyae, Cytherea sought
the Colchian; on the Caucasian crags Juno sat as watcher,
holding her dazzled gaze upon the Aeaean walls
between hope and fear, and as yet ignorant of what should come.
Scarcely had Venus, hidden, seen the first towers,
when, behold, a strange faintness begins to grip the maiden's
mind; her fevers redouble with renewed laments.
So once more, turning over her shifting thoughts about the stranger,
she grieves, and to him, absent, speaks such things in vain:
'If only your mother could help you now with Thessalian charms,
and—alas, if there is one—if any wife could help you.
What can I, a maiden, do but weep for your labors?
This is enough . . .
Ah me, lest I be forced even to watch your last hours,
and again to go as companion to my hard sister.
And now he thinks that no one is moved by his lot,
that no one remembers him, and with all the rest he hates
me too. Yet if ever there shall be any power in me,
that man—whatever last ash shall cling to the dreadful fields,
and the bones the bull and the savage fire shall have spared—
I will gather, and give a resting place. Then it shall be right
for me to have loved the hero's shade, and to render these cares to his tomb.'
She had spoken. Behold, Venus sat unforeseen upon the couch,
just as she was, transformed into the goddess and feigning, in painted
robes and with a magic wand, the Titan's daughter Circe.
The girl, as though deceived by the image of lingering sleep,
so holds her uncertain eyes, and little by little
thinks her the sister of her great father. Then, weeping for joy,
she sprang up and of her own accord gave kisses to the cruel goddess,
and spoke first: 'O at last, scarcely at last given back, harsh Circe,
to your own, what flight drove you from here with twin serpents?
Or what delay was dearer to you than your native shores?
Even before, the Thessalian keels sought the Phasis,
and unhappy Jason came in vain through so many shoals,
sooner than love of country moved you.' Then Venus breaks off
the rest and meets her: 'You are now the only cause of my journeys,
you alone; long since I come, made idle for your youth.
Spare the rest of your complaints, and do not blame me for following
the better course; for indeed the gifts of the gods will be claimed again.
Believe rather that this world is shared by all living things,
and the gods are shared. Call that your country, then,
where the day returns and goes, and let no grudging power, O child,
have shut us up forever under this one frost of one month.
It is right for me, and right for you, to leave the hostile Colchians.
And now I am the royal wife of Ausonian Picus,
nor do the pastures bristle for me there with fire-breathing bulls,
and you see me mistress of the Tuscan sea. But what suitors,
poor girl, are these Sauromatae of yours? To what Iberian do you go
(ah me), or to what savage Gelonian, no single bride?'
But the daughter had long since begun to spurn the goddess's words.
'You do not find me,' she says, 'so forgetful of great Perseis,
that I should be forced, unhappy, into such a marriage.
Go, I pray, and on my behalf dismiss that fear.
But rather, since you can, snatch this wretched girl from these cares,
whence comes my dread and fever, and the bitter things, O mother,
I have long endured, the burnings of a hard mind.
No rest for my soul, no sleep, the dry . . .
Seek some rest for my ills, and set my mind again in place,
give me back day and night, let me grasp the robes
that bring sleep, and with the wand itself compose my eyes.
You too help me nothing, mother; I was braver before,
alone. I see grim marriages and all things hostile,
and serpent locks rising upon your very head.'
Such words she gave, and, sinking down, wept in the lap
of cruel Venus, and showed the plague hidden in her bones
and the fire in the depth of her heart.
Venus seizes her in an embrace and plants frenzied
kisses, and breathes love mingled with hatred;
and while she encircles her grieving with shifting words
and holds her in other talk, 'But hear this,' she says,
'and raise your cheeks,' and thus, with tears welling up, she begins:
'When but now I glided down to you from the gods through the upper air,
by chance I saw a ship clinging to the first edge of the shore,
such as my island would never wish to send away from its harbor,
the island that still detains all sailors.
There one before all others, who then seemed to me
more beautiful than all (and I myself marveled long at their leader),
flies up, and thinking me one of your companions,
says: "By any power, if there is one—you who behold the dread
of a man about to die, one you would not see meet such undeserved
monsters—this I pray, this carry to the ear of your mistress maiden:
show her my tears; to her these words I send,
as I may, and these hands I stretch, as I can, from the shore.
The goddesses themselves, whom I dragged with me through a thousand perils,
have failed; my hope and only path of safety is what
she will give, if perhaps she gives it. Let her not reject my prayers,
not mine; and so many lives, such as she will never see again,
tell her, I pray, let her aid with her help, and save these names."
He poured it all out, and turning to look at the throngs of suitors
made known at once, at last he shuddered at his father's spheres,
and said: "If Minos's daughter herself gave her brother to death,
why should it not be right to help worthy strangers?
You too—bid the Aeaean fields grow gentle.
Let the Cadmean race fall at last in everlasting death.
Ah me, that here I can pay no thanks.
Yet let her know that this body, saved from cruel death,
this life, is her own. Will she then pity me?
Tell me," he says, "or rather—" and he rushed upon his drawn sword.
"I promised; do not fail me, I pray." And when I myself was moved
by the man's address and his plight, I let myself be entreated
rather than you; you are worthier of new praise, you of a worthy
suppliant; my fame is now enough won by my poisons.'
That girl had long been turning her eyes with a heavy face,
scarcely holding her spirit and her hand back from flying
into the very face of the speaking goddess: with such anger does shame
seethe, guarding its words; horror had seized her tender years.
And now upon her couch the unhappy girl buries her trembling ears,
and sees no way to carry her flight, no way to turn,
caught fast; she longs now to be buried and pressed down
by the broken earth, and to escape the dreadful words.
The goddess bids her follow, and waits in the very gates.
As savage Bacchus abandons Pentheus in the Echionian hall,
his horns wreathed about with dewy fillets dipped in dye,
when the man holds the god, and his mother's shame-bearing garments
and the drums, and the wretch suddenly takes the soft spear:
not otherwise, forsaken, she is afraid, and casts her eyes
all around through everything, and refuses to leave the house.
Against her is savage love, against her doomed Jason
presses, and the words she heard grow louder in her breast.
Alas, what is she to do? She sees herself, hard girl, betraying
her father to a foreign man, and now foresees the report
of her own crimes, and wearies the gods with lament, the gods
and Tartarus; she beats the ground and murmurs with crooked hands,
of the night, calling on Dis, that they at last be willing
to help her with death and send the man himself down to death too,
for whom she rages; absent, most savage, she demands
now Pelias, who with such wrath would destroy the young man;
often she resolves to promise the wretch her arts,
then refuses, and rather decrees that all be settled in one hour;
and she cries out that she will never yield to so base a love,
nor give aid and strength to a stranger,
and lies flung upon her couch—when she seemed to be called
again, and the doors sounded on their driven hinge.
So when she feels herself conquered deep within by some power
she knows not, and that whatever shame had warned before is cut away,
then she seeks the inmost chamber, seeking the greatest aids
she knew, on behalf of the king of the Haemonian keel.
And as from afar the chambers breathing with magic poisons,
and the cruel doors, lay open, and all things spread before her
that she had bought from the sea, from the deepest shades,
and what she had drawn from the bloody face of the moon,
'Then,' she says, 'will you follow, or suffer anything shameful,
when you have so many deaths and so brief an escape
from so great a crime?' Saying this, while no plague was swifter
than she through all the world, in vain she scans with all her sight
and lingers above it, and, about to die, gathers her wrath.
O day too sweet, the dearer at the very edge
of death: she stood, and marveled at her own raging.
'You are perishing, alas; can you bear this in your first youth?
You will see,' she says, 'no joys of the light, none of youth,
nor your brother's cheeks growing soft with their first down?
This man too, whoever he is, cruel girl, you do not know
perishes by your death—Jason, who now calls on you alone,
who entreats, and whom I first saw on our shore?
Why did it please you then to join treacherous hands,
father, and not at once to destroy the young man with these monsters?
I myself, I confess, even then, even then I wished it.
I call to witness your words, dear Circe, daughter of the Titan,
with you leading I follow, your counsels weary me,
aged one, and I yield, the lesser, to your warnings.' When she had said this,
again to the care and the fear of the Haemonian youth
she turns, glad to live for his sake alone,
or to die, whatever he should wish. She prays for greater
spells, for Hecate to send greater powers
upon her now, nor did she stand content with her known poisons.
Then her bosom is girded, and—where no force is more faithful
to her—she draws forth the flower of Prometheus's blood,
the Caucasian flower, and the herbs nourished by his torment,
which the sacred gore hardens and feeds amid the snows
and grim frosts, when the vulture, its flesh devoured,
rises from the crags and sprinkles dew from its open beak.
This same blood does not droop within the bounds of long age,
flourishing immortal; this same blood stands against the lightning,
and the herbs bloom in the midst of fire.
First Hecate brought the sickle hardened in Stygian springs,
and dug the mighty stalks from the rocks;
then the harvest was shown to her handmaid, which, ripened by Phoebe's lamp
under the tenth orbit, she reaps, and rages through all
the remnants and the gore of the god; he groans in vain,
gazing at the Colchian's face; then all his limbs draw together
with pain, and all his chains tremble beneath the sickle.
With such poisons the unhappy girl arms herself against her own realm,
and trembling enters the dark night.
Venus gives her hand, and, fearful, mingles coaxing kisses
with her words, and with joined step draws her through the walls.
As a mother, pale at the last, has led her tender brood
from the high nest out into the air,
and urges them to follow and rise on their short wings;
the first horror of dark Olympus strikes them,
and now they beg to return, and seek their accustomed tree:
not otherwise through the walls of the blind city she fails,
advancing, and dreads the silent houses, Medea.
Here again, on the threshold of the outermost gate, in vain
she stopped, and again her courage and her resolve dissolved,
and she looked back at the goddess, and clung a moment to these words:
'Does Jason himself ask for me, does he himself implore me?
Is there no fault beneath it? No stain upon my modesty,
no love, nor shame for a man to serve one who entreats?'
The goddess answers nothing, and breaks off the empty words.
And now already through the dark silence the Colchian
had begun to go with magic sound, and to hide the faces
of the mountain powers, and turn the rivers aside with their hills.
Now upon the stalls and flocks fear, upon the tombs a din,
had fallen; night herself stands amazed, slowed by heavy shade;
and now trembling Venus follows from afar; and when they had come
beneath the high beams and into the shade of the triform goddess,
here suddenly before her eyes, not yet hoped for, Jason
flashed out, and the terrified maiden saw him first,
and from here the daughter of Thaumas, in flight, raised herself
on her winged wings, and from there Venus slipped from the hand that held her.
As when in the late night a panic flings the herdsmen
and the flock together, or as through the deep void
blind shades without voices meet one another,
so, no otherwise, in the midst of the darkness of night and grove
they had fallen upon each other, both astonished, and drew near,
like silent firs or motionless cypresses
that the swift south wind has not yet stirred.
So, as each stood with downcast face in silence
and night went on its way, Medea longs at last to lift
her face and to be the first to speak to Aeson's son.
As soon as he saw her, trembling, with tears poured out
and burning cheeks and wretched shame,
he gave at last these words and consoled the loving girl:
'Do you bring any hope of light?' he says; 'do you come, I think,
pitying my toil? Or will you yourself rejoice at my death?
Do not, I pray, O maiden, bear yourself like your unspeakable
father; harshness ill befits such a face.
Was it fitting that these thanks, these awaited gifts of my labors,
be given thus? That I be sent back with you as witness—
is it right, O maiden? Grant to my words just hearing:
tell me, what did your father mean by setting me against such monsters,
what had I deserved, or why did he wish me to pay such penalties?
Is it because Canthus now lies dead by a foreign spear,
and because my Iphis fell before your walls,
or so great a band of Scythia thence? He should have bidden me go,
the treacherous king, and yield his realms to me at once.
By what perils, and on what terms, he gives back the hope
he promised, you see. We can at last die,
and that is settled, rather than undergo whatever
commands your father gives; never without the fleece will I depart
from here, nor will you be the first to see me a coward.'
So he speaks. She, trembling, when she sees the suppliant's face,
the man fallen silent, and now her own words demanded,
sees not, distraught, with what to begin, nor in what order,
nor how far, longing to pour out everything at the first
word; but shame gives no first words to her fear;
she falters, and scarcely lifting her eyes at last she speaks:
'Why, I pray, have you come into our land, Thessalian?
Whence any hope of me for you? And these great labors,
why did you not yourself, trusting in your own valor, attempt?
Surely, if I had feared to leave my father's house,
you had perished; surely tomorrow a cruel death awaited
this life of yours. Where now is Juno, where now the Tritonian maid,
since I alone am present to you in such great straits,
a queen of a foreign house? You yourself marvel too,
I think, and these woods do not now know Aeetes' daughter.
But I am conquered by your fates; take, a suppliant, the gifts
that are not mine; and if Pelias seek again to destroy you,
and send you into other perils, to other cities,
alas, do not trust to your own beauty.' And now the Titan's daughter
had begun to bring from her bosom the herbs and the Persean
powers, and again she addresses Jason with these words:
'Yet if you place any hope either in these gods
or in your own valor to lead you out from present death,
if perhaps it can, even now I beg you, stranger,
let me be, and send me back, innocent, to my wretched father.'
She had spoken: at once (for the ripe stars were not yet
rushing down, and Bootes still sufficed at the edge of the sky),
with a groan and much weeping she sets the charms before the youth,
as if, all at once, she casts away her country and her fame and her honor.
He takes them in his hand and seizes all their power.
Then, when the shame that makes her guilty and is never to be recalled
yielded from her face, and a nearer Fury filled her,
she now rolls the charms and fixes them through all the limbs
of Aeson's son, and over his whole shield is borne
with a sevenfold murmur, and gave the man a heavier spear,
and now the bulls' fires grow faint while they are absent.
'Now come, take up these crests and this helmet,'
she says, 'which but now Discord held in her death-dealing hand.
Hurl it through the midst of the crop, when you have ploughed the field;
at once the whole phalanx will go, turned against itself
in frenzy, and the father himself, raging, will marvel, and on me
perhaps will look.' Then, having spoken thus,
more and more she bore her mind over the high seas,
and now she saw the Minyae spreading their sails
without her. Then indeed, struck with the final grief,
she seizes Aeson's son by the right hand and humbly speaks:
'Be mindful of me, I pray; I in turn will remain mindful
of you, believe me. How far will you be from here, tell me, I pray, of the deep?
What quarter of the sky shall I behold? But let some care for me
touch you too, in whatever place, through whatever years;
and may you wish to remember that it was you, and to confess
my gifts, nor be ashamed to be saved by a maiden's art.
Ah me, why do no tears wring your eyes?
Or do you hide from me that I shall soon die, deserving it,
by my father's wrath? You the happy realms of your people,
you a wife and children await; I shall go forth, betrayed;
nor do I complain, and for your sake I will even gladly leave the light.'
At once the stranger to this (for with silent chants
she had bent him and long since breathed a like love into him)
says: 'Do you believe that Aeson's son could wish anything,
left behind, or endure any place without you? Give me back
rather to the tyrant, take back your thankless chants and strip them away.
What love of the light have I? Why should I wish for my country more,
if my father Aeson does not embrace you too first,
and Greece, rejoicing, watches you shining afar with your fleece,
and sinks down at the first waves to meet you?
Look upon these words, and now, I pray, consent, my bride.
By you, who are more powerful than the gods above and below,
and by these stars that return at your nod, O maiden,
and by these hours of our peril I swear:
if ever I should be forgetful of this deserving night,
if you should perceive that you have left scepter, home,
and parents, and that I then keep not these my promises,
then may it profit me nothing to have escaped the bulls
and the fierce earth-born, then may your fire and your arts
trouble me in my very house; let no man be able to aid
one ungrateful, and if there be anything then crueler than this,
may you add it, and leave me in the midst of terror.'
She heard him, and at once the Fury, ever the avenger
of lovers' complaints, pledged perjury to its deserved penalties.
When these words were said, yet both stand fixed,
and now they lift their faces, glad with bold youth,
faces that as often steal away each other's sweet glances,
now sick shame casts down their looks, and a delay is given
to their words, and again the maiden terrifies Jason:
'Hear what perils await you next, the bulls once tamed,
and what guardian remains to you at the Aeolian fleece;
not yet, I confess, have I fulfilled for you all I promised.
A toil more savage remains in the mighty tree of Mars,
believe me—would that there were such trust in me
and in nocturnal Hecate, and in my power . . .'
She had spoken, and that she might teach the man what monsters remained,
straightway she troubles the serpent reclining in vast coils,
and suddenly casts before it the shade of the Haemonian leader.
It—a thing it had never done—stood up and shot out its trembling
hisses, and after, in fear, it raised itself about its fleece,
and all the tree shuddered with its coils,
it begins then to follow, and rages through the air with empty jaws.
'What crash is this? What ruin so great, tell me, maiden?'
cries Aeson's son, standing cold with drawn sword.
She, laughing, draws him on, and at last, the snake checked, says:
'This my father's wrath prepares for you as the last,
alas, poor man, alas, dear to me again at such great perils.
O would that I were to see you through no labor at all
face the ash tree foul with its dark coils,
and trample the very eyes of the ever-watchful monster:
may it then befall me to die twice over.' So speaking she fled,
and bore herself back into the city beneath the last shadows.
And now empty hope had raised the king at the crimson
dawn, to learn through what waves one night had carried
Aeson's son, whether his face was free now on the open straits,
and whether, as before, the whole sea was silent. And while he tries
to explore that from afar, Arcadian Echion comes toward him
bearing word: that already on the Circaean fields of Mars
the man stands, and bids that the bronze-footed bulls be given for battle.
. . . and 'See, I am summoned of their own accord,' he said, 'and hope has lent me wings.
You now for the first time, O bulls, turn into flames for me
the plains; now open and roll out all your blasts.
Let the memorable harvest come forth for the Haemonian husbandman,
and you, my daughter, give your serpent to the Greek, your father's.
At his very sight let them perish upon the fleece, and let the hide
itself, stained, keep the dread gore for me.'
He speaks, and bids the plains be opened by the loosed bulls.
Some come up bearing the monstrous seeds of the Echionian
tooth, some carry the heavy timber of the dread plough.
But his own Pagasaean youth, on the other side, escort
the great-hearted man and throng about their leader; then each
gave his greatest words, and from afar withdrew into the savage fields.
He had set his stride, and out of the whole company alone
he stood, like one left by his farthest comrades,
whom the weary day and the burning sands of the south now—
or as one who, standing again toward the Riphaean heights,
the snow and the fierce horror of dark Boreas has carried off—
when suddenly the long wave of astonished Phasis,
and the Caucasian beams, and all the Aeaean land,
flashed, and the stalls poured forth their burning darkness.
And as, when from a single cloud, gleaming Jove
has hurled his twin fires upon mortals,
or when two winds at once have burst their bonds
and given themselves to flight: so then from their pen each
bull escaped, and breathed forth flames in a monstrous whirlwind,
lofty, and rolling its fires in a black tide.
The legion of the Argo's ship shuddered, the bold Idas shuddered,
who but now wept to be saved by a maiden's chants,
and looked toward the Colchian with unwilling face.
Jason himself did not bear the delays, and flung himself in;
after he sees them go apart, he shakes the threatening helmet
and with his right hand rouses the wandering fire to meet him.
. . .
. . .
Having hesitated a little, suddenly it rages. Not so do the seas,
angry, rush upon the rocks and recede again,
broken, backward. Twice with lightning blasts it bears down
and clouds the man over, but the Colchian does not let
the fires breathe upon him, and the cold flame is dashed
against the shield, and the fire pales at the sight of the poison.
Aeson's son thrusts in his right hand and lays hold of the burning
horns, then, leaning with all his strength, he clings.
That bull, refusing the man and then you too, Medea,
shakes him, and bears him, strained though he is by all the wrath
of the chant, yet helpless; at last, receding, it begins
to bellow more heavily, and, conquered, to lower its weary horn.
From here Aeson's son looks back at his comrades, demanding the huge
fetters, and now grips its mouth and is dragged, and drags,
and, straining on his knee, overcomes it and forces the trembling
muscles beneath the bronze yokes. Then the turbulent Colchian
disarms the other, and offers it sluggish and feebly threatening,
and as he draws near wraps it in night; it, fainting,
falls forward upon its head and shoulders by the very weight of its mass
and its rage. Jason rushes in, and presses with his whole
weight from above, and forces it, fixed, beneath his breath,
and when he had given it to the chains and bound it to the strong plough,
he raises it himself with his knee and drives it on besides with the cruel spear,
just as if from the midst of an opening in the earth
the back of a fresh-made horse, and the first murmur, broke
upon him with the reins, and the Lapith appeared on the height of Ossa.
He, as though he were cutting the fields of Libya and the rich
farmlands of fertile Nile, so with full hand rejoices
to scatter the seeds over the fields and loads the new furrows with war.
Here the warlike clangor of Mars first, thrice poured forth by the very
share, and from every furrow the horns rang out;
then the battle-clod is shaken, and at once a phalanx
is created and armed, and rises over all the fields.
The hero withdrew and drew back a little toward his comrades,
waiting where the first ranks the earth should give him.
But truly, when he saw the country now retreat from the topmost
crests, and saw them brandishing the earth from their menacing helmets,
he flies up, and where the ground lies nearest the lowest neck,
and the shoulders have not yet seen the day, he first with the pursuing sword
levels the trunks to the ground; the gleaming breastplate of the next,
or the first hands from their mother, he presses, meeting it before,
nor for those thousands or these beyond does he
suffice, more than when the Tirynthian, wearied at the dread hydra's
ranks, looks back to the Palladian fires.
So once again he turns to the Colchian's friendly arts,
and scatters the helmet's fastenings and the bonds at its rim,
yet he hesitates, and himself longs to meet the whole
war; no hope is given, so on every side the earth-born
leaders crowd their standards, and the shout and the trumpets.
And now all see the man, now all their weapons against him
flash. Then indeed, frantic at so great a crisis,
the helmet which Medea but now with Tartarean poison
. . .
he hurled into their midst; at once their spears were turned about.
As when the yearly wrath of the mournful Mother lacerates
the astonished Phrygians, or Bellona tears her gashed long-haired priests,
no otherwise Medea suddenly entangles the kindled
cohorts and drives the wretched brothers into her own battles:
there each thinks he lays Aeson's son low, in all of them
such wrath there was. Aeetes is amazed, and of his own accord
longs to call the raging men back, but all the ranks
lay fallen, nor did anyone rush first or any survive
above the rest, and suddenly the earth drank down its own slain.
Straightway into the river, his arms smoking, flies
Aeson's son, as Mars from Getic dust
enters on his horses and scorches the Hebrus heavy with sweat,
or as the black Cyclops from his caverns, and from the heat
of the ruddy lightning, when he rages and gasps in the Sicilian sea.
Restored here at last, and embracing his exulting comrades,
he no longer deigns to demand of the lying king the promised reward;
nor, if the king should of his own accord throw himself at his feet,
he who made the pact, would Jason wish to return to peace and the clasped hand
any longer; both fierce, both withdrew uttering threats.

title: Argonautica
text:
8. The Argonautica of Gaius Valerius Flaccus, Book Eight.
But the Colchian girl, trembling in her chamber and now dreading her own deeds,
the furies and the threats of her father, all alike, hold fast on every side;
no longer is there fear of the dark sea before her,
no land too far for the wretch; through whatever waves
she longs to carry her flight, whatever ship to board,
weeping she then gave her last kisses to her maiden fillets,
and embracing the couches she flees, she plucked her hair and cheeks,
and before . . . she snatched the traces of vanishing sleep,
and, pitiable, she moaned thus upon the pressed bed:
'O if to me, a fugitive, you would now give your last
embraces, Aeetes, my father, and would see, behold,
my tears. Do not believe, father, that he is dearer,
the one I follow; would I were overwhelmed at once by the swelling waves.
You, I pray, may you soon bear in peace this scepter, safe
through long old age, and may your other children be better to you.'
She spoke, and from the death-bearing caskets brings forth the charms
never to be scorned by a Haemonian husband,
and entwines her maiden bosom and her very necklace with poisons,
and added over all the savage sword.
Then, roused as though by the Furies' twisted scourge,
she leaps forth, as with frantic foot Ino leaps forth
into the seas, and, terror-struck, does not remember her little son,
whom she holds; her husband, in vain, strikes the farthest Isthmus.
Already the hero had come first into the grove, urged on by his cares,
and was hiding himself in the sacred night of the wood,
then too shining from afar with the starry beauty of his youth.
As, while still his companions' bands are scattered through the wilds,
the Latmian hunter rests in the summer shade,
worthy of a goddess's love, and now with veiled horns
the Moon comes: such, through the clouds, the leader
fills the grove with rosy glory and awaits such a lover.
But behold, the maiden, after the manner of a frightened dove,
which, surrounded by the vast shadow of the bird above,
trembling falls upon whatever man she may—no otherwise she,
driven by heavy fear, flung herself into his midst; but he
caught her, and first thus spoke with coaxing words:
'O great glory, you who shall come into our home,
and the only maiden found, not unworthy to be the cause
of such great journeys for a leader, I now require no
fleece at all, and it is enough that my keel has sought you.
But come, add this too, since you can, to your so great
gifts and services; for we were bidden to bring back
the golden hide; that glory touches my comrades.'
So he speaks, and a suppliant gives kisses to her first palms.
In answer the maiden began again with fresh sobs:
'I leave my father's house for your sake, and the wealth of my kin;
nor do I now speak as a queen, and, my scepter forsaken,
I follow my vows: keep this faith for me, a fugitive—the faith
you yourself gave first (you know it). The gods are present at our words,
the stars too behold both you and me. With you the seas, with you
I will try whatever roads, only let no day by chance
bear me back here, dragged off, and thrust me before my father's eyes;
this I beg of the gods above, this of you too, my guest.'
This she says, and frenzied she is borne off with swift step
through pathless places. He clings, her companion, and pities her as she goes,
when suddenly he sees a vast flame amid the clouds,
and the darkness quivering with cruel light.
'What is that redness of the sky? What so mournful a star
has flashed?' he says. To his alarm the maiden answers thus:
'You see the very eyes and grim lights of the dragon;
he shoots these flashes from his crests:
patient, he sees me alone before him and calls of his own accord,
as is his wont, and with coaxing tongue demands his food from me.
Tell me now, whether you wish to carry off the spoils
from one waking and seeing his foe, or whether we plunge
his eyes in sleep and hand you the serpent tamed instead?'
He is silent: so great a horror then came over the maiden.
And now the Colchian had stretched her hand and her hair toward the stars,
pouring out her chants in barbaric measure, and calling on you,
Father Sleep: 'Sleep almighty, you the Colchian summons from all
the world, and bids you now go to a single dragon,
I who have often tamed the straits with your horn, and the clouds
and lightnings and whatever flashes in all the upper air; but now,
now come, greater, and most like to your brother Death.
You too, most faithful guardian of the Phrixean ram,
it is time at last to turn your eyes from this care.
What treachery do you fear with me standing by? I myself
will keep the grove a while; meanwhile, lay aside your long labor.'
He, wearied, does not bear to depart from the Aeolian gold
nor to give his face to the rest allowed him, however welcome;
and, struck by the cloud of the first slumber,
he shuddered and shook the sweet sleep from the tree.
Against him the Colchian persists in foaming with Tartarean poisons
and in shaking all the silence of the Lethean branch,
and she overwhelms his struggling eyes with opposing chant,
and wearies with tongue and hand all the Stygian power,
until sleep at last seizes his burning rage.
And now the high crests have fallen, and the head, compelled,
now nods, and the huge neck droops outside its own fleece,
as the Po flowing back, or the Nile flung out into its seven streams,
or Alpheus coming into the Hesperian world.
After Medea herself saw the head of her dear dragon
upon the ground, flung about it with outstretched arms,
cruel nursling, she wept for him and for herself at once:
'It was not thus that in the late night I used to see you,
bringing you offerings and feasts, nor thus to your gaping mouth
did I give honey and faithfully feed you with my poisons.
How you lie now under a heavy bulk, how a sluggish
breath holds you helpless; nor did I even slay you, poor wretch.
Alas, you who must suffer the cruel day: now you will see no
fleece, no shining gifts of yours beneath your shade.
Yield then, and pass your old age now in other groves,
forgetful, I pray, of me, and let not your hostile hisses
drive me over all the sea. But you too, dismiss all delays,
son of Aeson, and flee with the fleece snatched away.
I, the guilty one, have quenched my father's bulls;
I have given the earth-born to their fates; behold, you have
the dragon's body laid low, and now, I hope, I have done with every crime.'
Then to him, who asked the way by which the towering hero
might bear himself to the head of the gold-bearing tree, 'Come, over the dragon
himself climb,' she says, 'and set your steps upon his prone back.'
There is no delay. Trusting her words, the offspring of Cretheus
treads on it and, though it is high, is carried to the airy ash,
whose branches still kept the ruddy hide,
like clouds set alight, or as when, her robe ungirt,
the daughter of Thaumas glides down to meet burning Phoebus.
Aeson's son seizes the longed-for glory and his last labor,
and the tree, borne by it through long years,
scarcely gave back with a groan the memorials of Phrixus's flight,
and grim darkness gathered over them.
Having gone out, they retrace the fields and seek the topmost
banks of the river. The whole field gleams, and now over all his limbs
he spreads the hide shaggy with starry tufts,
now draws it back to his neck, now wraps it about his left arm.
Such, from the Inachian caverns of Nemea, the Tirynthian
went, still fitting the lion's skin to his shoulders and head.
But when to his comrades, who then held the appointed
harbor, he appeared golden through the long shadows,
a shout rises from the Haemonian band; the ship too, rejoicing,
moves itself forward to the first banks to meet the youth.
He drives his steps headlong, and first flung the golden
hide aboard; then with the astonished maiden he leaps onto the ship
and stands, a victor, leaning on his snatched spear.
Meanwhile a savage horror came to her father's ears,
bearing the fate of his house and grief, and the deceit and the flight
of the maiden. From here the brother, in sudden arms . . .;
the whole city too soon gathers; Aeetes himself flies, forgetful
of his age, and the shores are filled with war
in vain; for the ship flees with reins let loose.
Still the mother stretched both her palms toward the seas,
and the sister, and all the others, the matrons and the young wives
of Colchis, and the girls your equals in age, Medea.
The mother alone stands out and fills the air with her wailings.
'Stop your flight, bring back the ship here from the midst of the sea,
daughter, you can. Where,' she cries, 'do you go? Here is all the throng
of your own, and a father not yet angry; here is your land
and scepter. Why do you trust yourself alone to Achaean lands?
What place is there for you, barbarian, among the daughters of Inachus?
Are these the vows of your house, the awaited marriage?
For this did I, aged, long for this day? Would that with hooked claws,
like a bird, I could go into the very face of the robber
and over his ship, and with a clear cry demand back
her whom I bore. This girl was promised to the Albanian tyrant,
not to you; in nothing did her wretched parents make a pact with you,
son of Aeson; Pelias does not bid you escape by this theft
or lead away, you Colchian, any of our daughters.
Take the fleece, and accept whatever is left from our temples.
But why do I accuse anyone with undeserved complaints?
She flees of herself, and (monstrous) of herself burns with so great a love.
This it was, unhappy woman—for the details come back to my mind one by one—
ever since the Thessalian kings came to the Colchian girl,
that no feast, no time, gave you pleasure, daughter.
You had then no color, and sick words,
and wandering cheeks, and your joys were always
in another's face. Why was so great a plague not disclosed to me,
so that Aeson's son might settle as son-in-law in our hall
and you not suffer such a flight; it would have been a shared crime,
or at least every crime now; we would both go
on whatever roads. It would have been a joy to seek together
Thessaly and whatever is the city of the savage stranger.'
So the mother, and the sister fills all with like complaint,
shrieking aloud; the handmaids alike, with a last cry,
give their words to the empty winds and call their mistress back
by name; far off the winds and your fate were bearing you away.
From there they fly a day and a night. To the returning men the breeze
is more welcome, and known lands run past the Minyae,
when suddenly Erginus speaks thus from the high stern:
'You,' he says, 'son of Aeson, content with the captured fleece,
see neither what way remains nor what fortune.
For tomorrow's day calls us to the borders of the savage sea
and the Cyaneae, and I remember, O Tiphys, your toils
among those rocks, father, I remember, O reverend one.
Our course must be changed, O comrades; another way of the sea
must be struggled through, and we must go by the course I shall tell.
Not far from here the vast outlet of the Scythian Hister rushes,
which, we are told, the rivers pour out by no single mouth;
it issues by seven waters, opens seven mouths.
Let us now seek the face of it, against the stream, and the wave
that falls into the left side of the sea; from there we will follow
the course of the river itself, until it carries us by a sure channel
and gives us back into another sea. Come, let any delays
be worth so much, son of Aeson, rather than to undergo again
the cruel rocks, than to break through the Cyanean mountains;
enough for me: behold, Argo does not return with all her garlands.'
This he says, not knowing that the cliffs now stand fixed
by a god's will and no longer clash with opposing rocks.
Aeson's son answered: 'You too, most faithful steersman,
no idle fears have touched, nor do I refuse to go
farther and to show myself, returning, to all lands.'
At once from there they turn aside to other kings and other places,
and seek the sea familiar to migrating wagons.
Far back on the stern, behind the watchful master,
Medea had clung to the knees of golden Minerva;
and there, sitting with her mantle drawn down over her eyes,
she still wept, although she went with Haemonian kings,
yet alone, and not secure of the marriage to come.
The shores of the Sarmatian sea pity her,
she passes, bewept, by the temple of Thoantean Diana.
No marsh, no river of Scythia but mourns her going;
seen, she stirred the Hyperborean frosts,
she who but now held so many kingdoms; the Minyae themselves
now lay aside their murmurs, now wish to bear her. Scarcely does she lift her face
to the late feasts, if ever, which dear Jason
himself was giving, signaling now that they pass cloud-bearing Carambis,
now the realms of Lycus, and so often, as she groans,
he beguiles her into rising at his urging toward the Haemonian mountains.
The island Peuce stands, named for a Sarmatian nymph,
where grim Hister, ever to be feared on either bank,
descends into the straits through his savage nurslings.
On this shore at last the leader resolved to loose his lingering cares,
and first he dared to teach his comrades of his pact
and the promised faith of marriage and the bond of wedlock.
Of their own accord all gladly urge him on and confess she has deserved it.
He himself now raises altars to unwilling Pallas,
and begins not to scorn the godhead of the Idalian goddess,
and beautiful above all, if ever, in the season
of his own marriage, he stands out among the Minyae as never more:
such as victorious Gradivus, from the bloody Hebrus,
